title: Airway Assessment and Preparation
summary: Recognise features of a potentially difficult airway and prepare equipment and steps for a safe intubation.
scenario: You are assisting the anesthesiologist before general anesthesia. Your task is to recognise airway risk, prepare the equipment, support the intubation sequence and respond correctly when confirmation of tube placement fails.
objectives: Recognise findings that predict a difficult airway
Prepare primary and backup airway equipment
Follow a safe airway preparation sequence
Respond to absent capnography after intubation

patient.procedure: Elective hernia repair under general anesthesia

references.title: Practice Guidelines for Management of the Difficult Airway

steps.title: Airway examination
steps.instruction: Select ALL findings that suggest a potentially difficult airway.
steps.prompt: The examination findings are listed below. Which ones raise concern?

items.label: Mallampati class III
items.why: Poor visualisation of oropharyngeal structures can predict difficult laryngoscopy.

items.label: Thyromental distance about 5 cm
items.why: A short thyromental distance can predict a more anterior larynx and difficult view.

items.label: Limited neck extension
items.why: Limited extension makes it harder to align the airway axes.

items.label: Full beard
items.why: A beard can prevent a good mask seal during bag-mask ventilation.

items.label: Mouth opening about 4 cm
items.why: Adequate mouth opening; not a risk factor.

items.label: Intact natural teeth, none loose
items.why: Normal dentition is not a risk indicator.

steps.explanation: Mallampati III, short thyromental distance, limited neck extension and a full beard are recognised risk indicators for difficult laryngoscopy or mask ventilation. Adequate mouth opening and intact teeth are not concerns.
steps.takeaway: Look for combinations of risk indicators, not a single sign.

steps.title: Planning
steps.situation: You have identified several risk indicators for a difficult airway.
steps.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Tell the anesthesiologist about the findings and make sure backup airway equipment is ready before induction
Proceed as routine and deal with problems only if they appear
Decide the airway plan after the patient is asleep

steps.explanation: Difficult airway guidelines stress recognising the problem early and having a strategy and backup devices prepared before induction. The plan is made by the anesthesiologist with the team.
steps.takeaway: Anticipate, communicate and prepare before induction.

steps.title: Prepare the airway station
steps.instruction: Select the equipment that should be prepared for this induction.
steps.prompt: Which items belong in the airway set-up for this patient?

items.label: Suction unit with rigid catheter, tested
items.why: Suction must be working before induction.

items.label: Bag-mask with oxygen source and well-fitting face masks
items.why: Needed for pre-oxygenation and rescue ventilation.

items.label: Laryngoscope handle and blades, light checked
items.why: A failed light is a preventable problem.

items.label: Endotracheal tubes: intended size plus one smaller and one larger, cuff tested
items.why: Sizes vary; the cuff must be tested before use.

items.label: Supraglottic airway as a backup device
items.why: A standard backup when intubation or mask ventilation is difficult.

items.label: Video laryngoscope available in the room
Chest drain kit
items.why: Not part of routine airway set-up.

items.label: Arterial line kit
items.why: Not needed for airway management in this patient.

items.label: Defibrillator pads applied to the patient
items.why: Defibrillator should be accessible, but pads are not applied for routine induction.

steps.explanation: The set-up includes suction, ventilation equipment, primary intubation devices in several sizes, backups such as a supraglottic airway and a video laryngoscope, and capnography. Items for other procedures are not needed.
steps.takeaway: Prepare primary AND backup devices, and test them before induction.

steps.title: Intubation sequence
steps.prompt: Arrange the steps around intubation in a safe order.

items.text: Check suction, laryngoscope light, tube cuff and bag-mask circuit
Pre-oxygenate with a well-fitted face mask
Assist the anesthesiologist with induction and tube placement
Confirm tube position: waveform capnography, chest movement, auscultation
Secure the tube and record its depth

steps.explanation: Equipment is checked first, then the patient is positioned and pre-oxygenated. Only then does induction and intubation happen, followed by confirmation of placement and securing the tube.
steps.takeaway: Check, position, pre-oxygenate, intubate, confirm, secure.

steps.title: No CO₂ waveform
steps.situation: The tube has been placed and connected to the circuit. The capnography shows NO waveform. Chest rise is unclear and SpO₂ is starting to fall.

options.text: Tell the anesthesiologist immediately that there is no CO₂ waveform, keep oxygenating and help re-check tube position as directed
options.consequence: The anesthesiologist knows at once and can reassess the airway while oxygenation is maintained.

options.text: Check the sampling line and connections yourself and report only if the problem persists
options.consequence: Checking connections is sensible, but delaying the report is unsafe when the airway may be misplaced.

options.text: Rely on chest auscultation and continue, because capnography is only a backup
options.consequence: Auscultation alone can be misleading. The tube may not be in the trachea and the patient is now desaturating.

options.text: Secure the tube with tape and wait a few minutes to see if CO₂ appears
options.consequence: Waiting delays recognition of a possible misplaced tube while oxygen levels fall.

steps.explanation: Absent end-tidal CO₂ after intubation means the tube must be assumed misplaced, or the circuit disconnected or obstructed, until proven otherwise. Waveform capnography is the most reliable confirmation of tracheal placement. Report at once and keep the patient oxygenated.
steps.takeaway: No waveform means no confirmation. Report immediately and keep oxygenating.

steps.title: Follow-up: falling SpO₂
steps.situation: SpO₂ is now 88% and still falling. The capnography waveform is still absent.

options.text: Call for urgent help, alert the anesthesiologist and support oxygenation while tube position is re-evaluated
Wait for the SpO₂ to recover on its own
Record the values and carry on preparing the drapes
Ask the surgeon to start so time is not wasted

steps.explanation: A falling SpO₂ with no confirmation of ventilation is an emergency. Calling for help early and supporting oxygenation is the priority.
steps.takeaway: Falling SpO₂ plus unconfirmed airway: call for help early.
